Our Verdict

Formal Data Generating Mechanisms, Likelihood Ratio Tests, 95% Confidence Intervals & Empirical Verdict

1. Data Generating Mechanism (DGM) Formulations

To predict individual educational attainment (\(Y_{\text{educ}}\)) conditioned on socio-demographic origin traits, we establish two formal statistical Data Generating Mechanisms: a primary Multinomial Logistic DGM for categorical milestone tiers and an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) DGM for continuous schooling years.

1.1 Primary Categorical Outcome: Multinomial Logistic DGM

We model the conditional log-odds of an individual attaining educational tier \(k \in \{\text{Some College}, \text{Bachelor Degree}, \text{Graduate Degree}\}\) relative to baseline \(K_0 = \text{High School or Less}\):

\[\ln\left(\frac{P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X})}{P(Y_{\text{educ}} = K_0 \mid \mathbf{X})}\right) = \beta_{k0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_k^T \mathbf{X}\]

where \(\mathbf{X}\) represents the vector of statistically selected socio-demographic covariates:

\[\mathbf{X} = \Big[ \text{parent\_educ}, \text{incom16}, \text{sibs}, \text{childs}, \text{age}, \text{year}, \text{sex}, \text{race}, \text{res16}, \text{family16}, \text{born}, \text{parborn} \Big]^T\]

The predicted conditional probability \(P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X})\) across all 4 attainment levels is determined via the soft-max transformation:

\[P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_{k0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_k^T \mathbf{X}\right)}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{3} \exp\left(\beta_{j0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_j^T \mathbf{X}\right)}\]

1.2 Comparative Continuous Benchmark: Linear Regression DGM

As a comparative benchmark, we model completed years of schooling (\(Y_{\text{years}} \in [0, 20]\)) as a continuous conditional expectation:

\[Y_{\text{years}} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}^T \mathbf{X} + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

TipKey Parameter Interpretations
  • Parental Education Effect (\(\beta = +0.279\) years): Each additional year of average parental education increases respondent schooling by 0.279 years (95% CI: [0.271, 0.287], \(p < 0.001\)).
  • Childhood Income Effect (\(\beta = +0.169\) years): Each step increase in childhood income tier adds 0.169 years of completed schooling (\(p < 0.001\)).
  • Immigrant Family Advantage: Respondents with non-U.S. born parents achieve higher odds of college and graduate degrees (\(\text{OR} = 1.878\), 95% CI: [1.817, 1.941], \(p < 0.001\)).

3. Visualizing Uncertainty: Odds Ratio Forest Plot

To evaluate parameter estimates and quantify uncertainty visually, we build a point-range error-bar plot displaying multinomial Odds Ratios (\(\text{OR} = \exp(\beta)\)) alongside exact 95% Confidence Interval bounds for predicting Bachelor Degree and Graduate Degree attainment relative to High School baseline.

4. Formal Predictive Verdict

📊 Predictive Modeling Verdict & Key Summary

1. Goodness-of-Fit Metrics

  • Multinomial Model Deviance: 1.087047^{5}
  • Multinomial Model AIC: 1.088307^{5}
  • Linear Model \(R^2\): 0.3117 (Explains 31.17% of overall variance in schooling years)
  • Sample Size: \(N = 48,360\) complete cases across 52 GSS survey years (1972–2024).

2. Answer to Central Predictive Question

“To what extent do parental education, childhood income, family structure, geography, demographics, and birth cohort predict educational attainment?”

  1. Parental Education is the Dominant Factor: Every additional year of parental schooling multiplies the odds of earning a Bachelor’s degree by 1.333x (\(\text{OR} = 1.333\), \(p < 0.001\)) and a Graduate degree by 1.405x (\(\text{OR} = 1.405\), \(p < 0.001\)).
  2. Childhood Environment & Family Size: Higher childhood relative income (incom16) significantly boosts attainment odds (\(\text{OR} = 1.172\)), whereas larger sibling size (sibs) and non-intact family structures (family16) present conditional barriers.
  3. Generational Secular Expansion: Later survey cohorts (year) exhibit strong structural increases in degree attainment, reflecting nationwide higher education expansion.

3. Strategic Policy Recommendation

Because parental education and childhood economic status exert strong conditional effects on educational outcomes, state policy initiatives should combine targeted higher education tuition subsidies with family support programs to foster intergenerational socio-economic mobility.
